analysis.one_liner: Removes dollar caps on damages for victims of intentional employment discrimination.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a committee vote or a Senate vote; it died when the 110th Congress ended in January 2009.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, a worker who wins an intentional employment discrimination case can only recover a limited amount in compensatory and punitive damages — caps that run from $50,000 to $300,000 depending on the employer's size. This bill would delete those caps, letting juries award whatever amount fits the harm, the same way damages work in many other discrimination and injury cases. It also explicitly guarantees a jury trial on demand. The bill was referred to the Senate committee that handles labor matters and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who experience intentional discrimination on the job — based on race, sex, religion, national origin, disability, or age — and win their lawsuits. Removing the caps means a jury could award damages that match the actual financial and emotional harm, instead of an amount capped as low as $50,000 at small employers. It also benefits all workers indirectly by giving employers a stronger financial reason not to discriminate.

how_it_helps.text: Deletes the statutory cap on the combined compensatory (pecuniary and nonpecuniary) and punitive damages available for intentional employment discrimination under 42 U.S.C. 1981a, so awards are limited only by the actual proof of harm.
Replaces the existing damages scheme, which caps awards at $50,000 to $300,000 depending on employer size, with the same uncapped remedies available under other civil rights provisions.
Guarantees any party a jury trial in these cases, instead of leaving the request tied to the damages structure it amends.

analysis.who_pays: Employers found liable for intentional discrimination, who would face potentially larger jury awards and settlements. The bill amends 42 U.S.C. 1981a, which applies to employers covered by Title VII — generally private employers with 15 or more employees, unions, and employment agencies — plus federal sector provisions. Workers pay nothing directly; the cost of larger verdicts is borne by employers and, indirectly, may be priced into employment and liability insurance.

drawbacks.text: Employers and business groups have long argued that uncapped damages make discrimination lawsuits unpredictable and expensive, and could pressure employers into settling weak claims rather than fighting them — a cost that can fall on small businesses and, through pricing and hiring decisions, on workers generally. This objection is not in the provided sources but reflects the standard case for keeping caps, which the bill was written to remove.

The bill leaves no dollar ceiling at all, so an honest supporter would acknowledge that jury awards can vary widely by jurisdiction and that removing all caps gives judges less ability to correct outlier verdicts than a high cap would.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is concrete for a specific group: workers who prove intentional discrimination but are capped at $50,000-$300,000 regardless of the harm they suffered. The cost falls on employers as larger liability exposure, which is the point — making discrimination genuinely expensive is the mechanism by which the bill deters it. The main fair criticism is that total removal of caps, rather than raising them, trades predictability for deterrence, and that case outcomes could become more erratic. On balance it is a straightforward pro-worker remedy bill with a real but diffuse cost to business.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and referred to the Senate HELP committee in August 2007 and sat there with no hearing, no vote, and no floor action until the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Kennedy introduced the bill on August 1, 2007 with seven Democratic cosponsors — Dodd, Murray, Clinton, Obama, Leahy, Feingold, and Cantwell.
The Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions on the day it was introduced.
The action history shows no further activity: no committee markup, no committee vote, no floor debate, and no roll-call in either chamber before the 110th Congress ended on January 3, 2009.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers with 15 or more employees, who keep the current $50,000-$300,000 caps on discrimination damages, and the liability-insurance business that prices around those caps.

sides.party_line_note: There was never a vote, so no partisan split is recorded; all eight named supporters were Democrats, and no Republican support or opposition appears in the record.

industries.industry: Covered employers (private businesses with 15+ employees, unions, employment agencies)
industries.note: Removing the damage caps would expose employers to unlimited jury awards for intentional discrimination, raising both verdict risk and settlement values. Keeping the caps is worth real money to employers and leaves workers with compensation that can fall well below proven harm.

Uncapped awards would raise the ceiling on claims these insurers must pay, increasing premiums and exposure. This effect follows from the bill's removal of caps; the industry itself does not appear in the provided sources.
